content: Another thing I’m overly cautious about is that Comparator is still in the TCB of all these AI projects and having multiple kernels doesn’t help. There have been bugs in Comparator before that would let it be exploited (or so I remember). I’d be interested in a proof of correctness of the part of comparator which takes two export files, compares them, runs a kernel on them and also checks for axioms.
You could write a comparator comparator that runs multiple independent implementations of comparator.

Comparator isn’t as complicated as a Lean kernel, especially if we are only looking at the part that takes two serislized export files as input. I think if we could make a clear spec and formally verify that, it could go a long way. I’m not sure we need 6 different versions of comparator. cc @Henrik Böving If we have a truly trustworthy Comparitor and a truly trustworthy kernel, I think Lean would be in a much better place for low trust verification settings (like AI proofs of major theorems).

There is no simple specification that would have prevented the bugs in comparator. For example, a very important class of bugs is "do we export everything that the lean kernel considers a bultin" which requires answering the question "what is a built-in" for writing a spec. All of the previous bugs in this regard have been caused by answering this question wrong so the spec would also be wrong.
Note that this general class of bugs is of course eliminated by the use of alternative, verified kernels that do not rely on this.
Comparator also relies on sandboxing. I would expect that is one of the weakest points now; and mostly outside of comparator's control.

Very much correct yes, one would have to prove that there is no Linux system call that is left open by bwrap that allows an attacker to do things, which in turn also requires verifying parts of the Linux kernel.

Note that with the release that is being cooked as we speak we do open the possibility for you to build your export files wherever you want (for example in a VM) and then safely feed it into comparator. So if you are feeling really paranoid you could run a linux VM with lean in a verified hypervisor.

I’d like to push back on this:

  1. I think comparator has two parts. One is that it runs lean in a safe environment. And the second is that it checks the correctness of the outputted serialization. The first would be a nightmare to formally prove, but as you plan to do it also can be separated from the second. The second only concerns the serialized export files. That would be much more manageable.
  2. By proving certain properties about the serialized export files comparison, you would be making very clear what you expect from an external checker. (I apologize if I misunderstood and mischaracterized the previous bugs. But even if Comparator has never had a bug, having a proof that it is correct would be helpful for Lean’s trust story.)
  3. Here is one simple thing that one can rigorously prove about Comparator (the version which compares two serializations). “If a challenge declaration has a type of False, then there is no solution export file that could complete it with the three standard axioms.” Of course to complete the proof of this spec, one needs assumptions on the external kernel, but that is great because these are then obligations for the external kernel that can be proved of each verified kernel.
